title: How to cut a cake fairly for three people
description:
Cut and choose is fair for two: you cut so either half is fine for you, and your friend picks. For three it breaks: if you cut three pieces and Ben takes the frosted one Mia also wanted (half the cake to her), the two left are only a quarter each to her. The fix is a moving knife: slide it across the cake and the first person who thinks the slice is worth a third yells stop and takes it. Everyone else thought it was under a third, so the rest is worth over two thirds to them, and cut and choose between the last two gives each at least half of that. Everyone ends up with at least a third by their own measure (Dubins and Spanier, 1961).

Numbers checked in code: the cut-and-choose counterexample, and 100,000 random cakes with three people valuing it differently (nobody ever below a third by their own measure). Sources: Wikipedia, Proportional cake-cutting, Dubins-Spanier theorems, Selfridge-Conway procedure.

social_caption: Cut and choose is fair for two, but three people break it. Here's the moving-knife trick that guarantees everyone a third.
facts_checked: Mia values the frosted piece at 1/2 and the others at 1/4 each, so after Ben takes it her best is 1/4 < 1/3 while the cutter keeps 1/3; moving knife + cut and choose on 100,000 random cakes (three people, 12-slice random valuations): worst own share exactly 1/3, never below; the first to yell thinks someone else got at least as much (envy in nearly every trial); quiet people value the rest at 2/3 or more, half of 2/3 = 1/3; four friends yell at 1/4 (verify.py)

Moving-knife procedure: a knife moves from the left, any participant calls stop when 1/n of the cake lies to its left and takes that piece, repeat; Dubins and Spanier 1961, 'How to Cut a Cake Fairly' (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportional_cake-cutting, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dubins%E2%80%93Spanier_theorems)
Envy-free division for three needs a cleverer procedure: Selfridge 1960 / Conway, at most 5 cuts (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selfridge%E2%80%93Conway_procedure)

beats.say: Cut and choose: fair for two, broken for three.
Nobody cheats. Everyone plays honest, and it still breaks.
With two, you cut so either half is fine for you. Your friend picks. Nobody can complain.
Now three. You cut three pieces you think are equal. Ben grabs the frosted one. But Mia wanted that one too. To her, the two left are a quarter each.
So how does nobody, by their own eyes, end up with less than a third?
Slide a knife slowly across the cake. The moment anyone thinks the slice is worth a third, they yell stop and take it.
Everyone who stayed quiet thought that slice was smaller. So to them, the rest is worth more than two thirds.
The last two cut and choose. Half of two thirds is a third.
Everyone gets a third or more, by their own eyes. Dubins and Spanier, 1961.
